newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Volvo sells Renault stake for $740 mln.
newsitem.headline: Volvo sells Renault stake for $740 mln.

text.p: Sweden's AB Volvo's drive to turn into a slimmer, meaner machine continued on Thursday when it sold its stake in France's Renault as part of an ongoing campaign to focus on its own vehicle operations.

Although the sale was expected, analysts approved of the timing of the deal under which Volvo sold its 27.2 million Renault shares to the Union Bank of Switzerland for 5.9 billion crowns ($740 million) for a capital gain of 750 million crowns.
The stake, amounting to 11.38 percent of Renault's capital, was a left-over from a failed merger of the pair in 1993.
"This seemed a good time to sell," BZW analyst Andy Blair-Smith told Reuters.

"Volvo now has this money to plough back into new model development, expand truck operations in Eastern Europe, and to look for acquisitions in the U.S. truck market where Volvo is a potential bridegroom for Renault's Mack division."
Analyst Lars Glemstedt of Aros Securities agreed the timing was good, with the French auto maker's shares trading at around 171 francs on Thursday, up from 120 francs earlier this year.
"The company can now look for potential acquisition targets in its truck and construction equipment sectors," he said.

Volvo has pursued a divestment programme since early 1994, when then chief executive Soren Gyll began to strip down the seafood-to-stockbroking empire built up by his predecessor Pehr Gyllenhammar to concentrate on its core automotive businesses.
"The sale of our stake in Renault is fully in line with the strategy the board decided on at the start of 1994," Volvo current chief executive Leif Johansson said in a statement.
"We are selling now to realise the upturn in the Renault share in 1997, which has been further accentuated over the past week."
The sale leaves Volvo with just one major shareholding to dispose of -- a tranche of about four percent of troubled U.S./Swedish drugs company Pharmacia & Upjohn.
Volvo sold two thirds of its 14 percent P&U holding last summer, but Volvo spokesman Stefan Karlsson said there would be no more major disposals for the time being.
"It's not on the cards right now," he told Reuters.
Major spin-offs to date have included Swedish Match, which was paid out as a bonus dividend to Volvo shareholders in early 1996, and the Finnish food group Cultor.

Last month Volvo sold its 4.72 percent stake in SAS Sverige AB for a capital gain of 221 million crowns, and in early 1997 it saw a capital gain of 3.03 billion crowns from selling its shares in drinks group Pripps Ringnes to joint owner, Norwegian conglomerate Orkla.

The disposal programme has raised some 45 billion crowns since 1994 which Volvo has spent on a 5.2 billion crown share redemption programme, research and development, freshening up its dowdy image, and broadening its customer base.
Analysts said last year's launch of the S40/V40 midsize car range was a good start for the new look Volvo.
Volvo shares rose slightly after the announcement of the sale to trade two crowns higher at 214 crowns on a generally soft Stockholm bourse.
